messages.subject: specifying subgroup to polygon
parts:
Hi all,
I've just discovered ggplot2 and have been trying to figure something
out without success.
I found this code online and modified it a tad to ask this question.

df <- data.frame(x = rnorm(100), y = rnorm(100),
site = sample(letters[1:6], 100, rep = T))
ggplot(df, aes(x, y, colour = site)) + geom_point()
find_hull <- function(df) df[chull(df$x, df$y), ]
hulls <- ddply(df, "site", find_hull)
ggplot(df, aes(x, y, colour = site)) + geom_point() +
geom_polygon(data = hulls, fill = NA)


I would like to allow "site" to retain the task of coloring the
points. However, I need the polygons to form around a different subset
of the points.
For example, say there are six sites (as in the code) but three of
these sites were a control treatment while the other three were
experimental.
I would need two polygons, one for control and one for treatment.

I've tried adding the variable of interest ("stimulus") to the
data.frame and it adds just fine, the problem I'm having is not
knowing where to specify it in the rest of the code so that the
polygons are using that variable. With my actual data, I've tried
placing it in the obvious spot such as:

...hulls <- ddply(df, "stimulus", find_hull) ...

but the outcome is always way too many polygons and straight lines.
The polygons are still forming connections between like-colored points
but the polygons are different from the "site" polygons so something
is happening.

I apologize for being too ignorant to write code to create another
variable to make sure you see what I am seeing.

Thank you for any help!
-Teresa

> I would like to allow "site" to retain the task of coloring the

> experimental.

df <- data.frame(x = rnorm(100), y = rnorm(100),
site = sample(letters[1:6], 100, rep = T))

hulls <- ddply(df, "trt", find_hull)

ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
geom_point(aes(colour = site, shape = trt)) +
geom_polygon(data = hulls, fill = NA, colour = "grey50")

But I find this display extremely hard to read! It might be better in
a real example if the treatments were actually different though.

Thank you, Hadley! That is what I need. I want to try out this method of displaying results to illustrate that, in my data, there is mostly overlap but that where the groups differ it is being driven by single sites. Therefore, the important thing to note in the graph I produce will be the fact that all the points that deviate from the cluster are a single color (i.e., come from a single site). 
I'm looking at bird vocalizations (in response to different stimuli) and the driving force behind a purported difference is being driven purely by individuals sounding different from one another (the calls are not stimulus-specific).

Is there a way to specify that each hull be drawn in a different color? I've tried a few things but just get errors. As it is, there is a strange change in trajectory of the lines when they intersect. It's like a mobius strip!

Thanks, again!
-Teresa
